qt: to the Commission Dimitris Tsiodras (PPE) Subject:

Heating and cooling account for around half of energy consumption and still rely heavily on imported fossil fuels. At the same time, Europe is facing persistently high heating costs, with many households confronted with the consequences of the energy crisis. Solar thermal technologies manufactured in Europe, including in Greece, can help reduce energy bills and strengthen the EU’s energy resilience1. In view of the forthcoming action plan on cooling and heating and the revision of the directives on renewable energy (RED), energy efficiency (EED) and governance: 1.
How will it ensure that the plan will strengthen the development and production of European solar thermal technologies?

Will it consider setting quantified deployment targets and monitoring indicators for renewable heating technologies, in areas such as buildings, district heating networks and heat from industrial processes, and how will it ensure that these targets are reflected in the EU heating and cooling framework, including the above legislation?
How will it ensure that support mechanisms and financial instruments for clean heating remain accessible for solar thermal technologies?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.11.2026) Solar thermal technologies account for less than 1% of total EU heat consumption. Under the projections outlined in the REPowerEU plan1, unlocking the solar thermal potential could triple demand by 2030 with major benefits for energy security and for efficient decarbonisation of heating and cooling. The requirements for solar installations under Article 10 of the Energy Performance of Buildings Directive2 promote both solar thermal and hybrid photovoltaic-thermal systems. It is expected to drive an increase of solar thermal use in buildings of more than 50% by 2030. Renewable heat sources – including solar thermal – are promoted under the Renewable Energy Directive3, as well as the Energy Efficiency Directive4, driving renewable energy use in district heating and cooling. The Commission is working with national authorities to ensure the effective implementation of these rules. The Electrification Action Plan adopted in July 20265 also recognised the importance of direct renewable heat sources complementing electrification. The guidance on social leasing and support schemes attached to the Action Plan explicitly covers solar thermal.
